pages.title: Experiments
pages.lede: Five gates. One testable claim at each step.
pages.boundary: This migration contains an experimental blueprint, not completed experiments. Replace every planned condition with dated protocols, deviations, sample IDs, and result links.

facts.label: Order
facts.value: Later claims depend on earlier gates.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: Every assay tests a competing explanation.

facts.label: Record
facts.value: Protocols resolve to samples and notebook dates.

facts.label: Decision
facts.value: Advance only when acceptance rules are met.

sections.title: Five gates. No skipped claims.
sections.summary: A reporter signal cannot establish topology; topology cannot establish presentation; presentation cannot establish selective function.
body: The route is deliberately sequential. Every gate consumes named evidence from the previous gate and produces either an advance decision, a repeat condition, or a return to design. Ambiguous material should never be carried forward simply because a later assay produces an attractive signal.

items.label: Gate 01
items.title: Construct identity
items.body: Confirm insert boundaries, epitope order, linker logic, reading frame, backbone version, and critical junctions before RNA production.
evidence: An annotated sequence and plasmid map that identify every functional boundary.
Clone lineage, backbone version, expected products, and sample identifiers.
Chromatograms or equivalent confirmation for critical junctions and reading frame.
items.decision: Advance only when identity, orientation, and critical junctions resolve without an unexplained mixed signal.

items.label: Gate 02
items.title: Circular topology
items.body: Combine matched linear RNA, RNase R response, junction-specific detection, sequence confirmation, and purity assessment.
evidence: Junction-specific detection supported by sequence or orthogonal identity evidence.
Matched linear RNA and RNase R conditions processed in the same experimental batch.
Recovery, integrity, purity, and unresolved products reported beside the preferred band.
items.decision: Repeat, purify, or redesign whenever the evidence cannot distinguish circular product from resistant linear or concatemeric material.

items.label: Gate 03
items.title: Expression window
items.body: Measure uptake/process control, intended output, matched linear RNA, time, dose, and viability from aligned samples.
evidence: Matched input, delivery condition, dose, time point, and sample lineage.
A delivery or process control that separates failed access from failed translation.
Encoded output displayed beside viability and cell-state measurements.
items.decision: Do not advance a high-signal condition when the increase is inseparable from unacceptable stress, loss of viability, or batch imbalance.

items.label: Gate 04
items.title: Presentation evidence
items.body: Distinguish general activation from sequence-specific display using an irrelevant epitope, matched delivery conditions, and an assay that resolves the presented target.
evidence: A presentation-specific readout aligned to expression and cell-state controls.
Irrelevant epitope and antigen-negative conditions under matched delivery.
General activation measured separately from sequence-specific display.
items.decision: Presentation is supported only when the target-specific difference survives the irrelevant and process controls; expression alone is insufficient.

items.label: Gate 05
items.title: Selective recognition
items.body: Compare antigen-positive and antigen-negative targets beside functional and stress baselines before making any claim about selective response.
evidence: Antigen-positive and antigen-negative targets tested in the same assay window.
Functional response, non-specific stress, and baseline activity reported together.
Replicate structure and predefined exclusions that preserve the target comparison.
items.decision: Bound the conclusion to the tested target, assay, dose, and time window; reject a selectivity claim when general stress explains the response.

sections.title: Make the method reusable, not merely visible.
sections.summary: Each protocol records materials, critical parameters, deviations, attachments, and the exact evidence it is designed to generate.
body: A protocol is treated as a versioned research object. The question, comparator, acceptance rule, and required record are fixed before execution; actual deviations remain attached to the dated Notebook entry rather than being silently folded into a cleaner method.

items.label: PR–01
items.title: Construct assembly and verification
items.body: Backbone, insert boundaries, primers, expected sizes, assembly conditions, clone lineage, plasmid map, and chromatograms.
evidence: Versioned construct map, primer table, expected product sizes, and assembly conditions.
Clone identifiers linked to screening results and full sequence attachments.
Every deviation recorded in the dated Notebook execution rather than silently corrected.
items.decision: Release the protocol only when another team can reconstruct which material was built, screened, accepted, and carried forward.

items.label: PR–02
items.title: RNA production and topology
items.body: Transcription input, circularization route, cleanup, recovery, integrity, RNase R conditions, primer orientation, and junction trace.
evidence: Input template, transcription and circularization parameters, cleanup route, and recovery.
Primer orientation, expected junction product, enzyme conditions, and matched controls.
Raw gel, trace, or sequence files connected to the exact RNA batch.
items.decision: A reusable protocol must state the acceptance threshold and the corrective route for low recovery, degradation, contamination, or ambiguous topology.

items.label: PR–03
items.title: Delivery, expression, and viability
items.body: Cell source, passage, seeding density, dose, reagent, exposure time, viability method, normalization, and replicate structure.
evidence: Cell source and state, seeding density, formulation, dose, exposure, and harvest timing.
Delivery and expression readouts normalized with the same documented reference.
Viability, morphology, or stress measurements from aligned wells and samples.
items.decision: The method is reusable only when it exposes the operating window and the conditions that must be repeated, retuned, or rejected.

items.label: PR–04
items.title: Presentation and selective recognition
items.body: Presentation assay, target identity, matched negative and irrelevant controls, response readout, stress baseline, and predefined interpretation boundary.
evidence: Target provenance and antigen status documented before comparison.
Matched negative, irrelevant, process, and positive-control conditions.
Response and toxicity measurements linked to a predefined analysis version.
items.decision: The protocol must prevent a general activation signal from being reported as target-specific recognition.

note.label: Protocol boundary
note.body: A protocol describes what was done. The bounded conclusion and figure belong on Results; the dated execution record belongs in Notebook.

sections.title: Design controls before seeing the signal.
sections.summary: Controls define what a positive result can mean and prevent one attractive readout from carrying a stronger conclusion than the assay supports.
body: Controls are organized around alternative explanations, not around a generic checklist. Each experimental figure should make it possible to distinguish biological absence, process failure, background signal, non-specific activation, and the specific difference the experiment was designed to test.

items.label: Negative
items.title: Define background
items.body: No-template, no-RNA, mock delivery, and antigen-negative conditions establish assay and biological baselines.
evidence: Technical blanks and no-template conditions for instrument or reagent background.
Mock and no-RNA delivery conditions for process-associated response.
Antigen-negative biology tested under the same acquisition and analysis settings.
items.decision: A positive result must clear the relevant technical and biological baselines, not merely differ from an empty well.

items.label: Process
items.title: Locate failure
items.body: Delivery, extraction, amplification, staining, and instrument controls distinguish process failure from biology.
evidence: Process controls placed at the delivery, extraction, amplification, staining, and acquisition stages.
Acceptance criteria reported for every stage capable of erasing a biological signal.
Failed quality gates remain visible beside excluded or repeated samples.
items.decision: Interpret a negative biological result only after the controls show that the relevant process stages remained informative.

items.label: Comparator
items.title: Test the claimed difference
items.body: Matched linear RNA, irrelevant epitope, and alternative construct conditions challenge the preferred mechanism.
evidence: A comparator that changes the proposed mechanism while preserving unrelated handling variables.
Matched linear RNA, irrelevant epitope, or alternative construct conditions where appropriate.
The same measurement range, exclusions, and replicate logic applied across the comparison.
items.decision: The claimed mechanism is not supported when the preferred condition cannot be distinguished from a credible alternative explanation.

items.label: Reference
items.title: Verify that the assay can respond
items.body: A validated material or stimulation condition defines the expected direction and reveals when an apparently negative experiment is technically uninformative.
evidence: A positive-control material or stimulation with a documented expected direction.
Control performance shown for the same batch, acquisition window, and analysis pipeline.
A predefined response range that distinguishes weak biology from assay failure.
items.decision: When the reference condition fails, classify the experiment as technically uninformative rather than biologically negative.

next.label: Notebook
next.title: Where did each sample and decision come from?

pages.title: Notebook
pages.lede: Dates, samples, deviations, and decisions—one traceable record.
pages.boundary: No team notebook export was supplied. The entries below define the record schema and must be replaced with real dates, participants, files, and outcomes.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Date, time, project phase, and owner.

facts.label: What
facts.value: Purpose, procedure, samples, and deviation.

facts.label: Observed
facts.value: Raw observation before interpretation.

facts.label: Next
facts.value: Decision, follow-up, and linked evidence.

sections.title: Every entry should survive handoff.
sections.summary: A future reader should understand what happened without relying on the memory of the person who performed it.
body: Each entry begins with a question and ends with an assigned next action. Sample identifiers, raw files, protocol versions, and deviations are mandatory links, while interpretation is kept visually separate from the observation that produced it.

items.label: Context
items.title: Purpose and people
items.body: Date, owner, collaborators, research question, protocol version, and related design record.

items.label: Execution
items.title: Samples and deviations
items.body: Sample IDs, lineage, reagents, lots, equipment, parameters, environmental conditions, and departures from protocol.

items.label: Outcome
items.title: Observation and next step
items.body: Raw files, observations, interpretation, uncertainty, decision, responsible person, and follow-up date.

sections.title: Chronology with an evidence spine.
sections.summary: The final timeline should contain all project work, including unsuccessful builds, analysis changes, safety decisions, and meetings that affected experiments.
body: The timeline is not a highlight reel. Failed preparations, inconclusive assays, threshold changes, and pauses for safety or supervision remain part of the scientific record because they explain why the project changed direction.

items.label: NB–2026–01 · replace date
items.title: Construct definition and acceptance criteria
items.body: Reserved for the team meeting that freezes the candidate sequence, expected products, primer plan, and no-go conditions.

items.label: NB–2026–02 · replace date
items.title: Assembly and sequence review
items.body: Reserved for build conditions, clone IDs, deviations, chromatograms, failed clones, and the decision to advance or rebuild.

items.label: NB–2026–03 · replace date
items.title: RNA production and topology evidence
items.body: Reserved for sample lineage, recovery, raw images, junction evidence, ambiguity, and the next purification or geometry change.

items.label: NB–2026–04 · replace date
items.title: Assay review and continuation decision
items.body: Reserved for aligned readouts, control performance, uncertainty, team interpretation, the accountable reviewer, and the decision to advance, repeat, revise, or stop.

sections.title: One record, several destinations.
sections.summary: Notebook entries remain the provenance layer; other pages cite them rather than copying the daily log.
body: A single execution can support several downstream artifacts, but each artifact points back to the same source record. This prevents a figure, protocol, or design decision from becoming detached from the sample and analysis history that produced it.

items.label: EXP–xx
items.title: Protocol used
items.body: The exact protocol version and any deviations in this execution.

items.label: RES–xx
items.title: Result generated
items.body: The result block and raw file that use this sample or analysis.

items.label: DR–xx
items.title: Decision changed
items.body: The build, threshold, assay, or boundary that changed because of the record.

items.label: FIG–xx
items.title: Figure released
items.body: The plotted result, caption boundary, analysis version, and accessible source data created from the record.

next.label: Measurement
next.title: How will each readout remain comparable?

pages.title: Measurement
pages.lede: Calibration, controls, range, and uncertainty beside every result.
pages.boundary: The page currently defines the reporting and calibration plan. Instrument settings, standard curves, units, replicate counts, and validation results await team data.

facts.label: Meaning
facts.value: The readout resolves a named biological question.

facts.label: Range
facts.value: Limits of detection and quantification are stated.

facts.label: Compare
facts.value: Calibration and normalization remain explicit.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Replicates, error, and failed quality gates stay visible.

sections.title: Connect material, instrument, number, and decision.
sections.summary: Each measurement should show how a biological state becomes a recorded value and how that value supports a bounded decision.
body: The chain begins before the instrument is switched on. The team first names the biological quantity, the competing explanation, and the useful range; calibration, acquisition, normalization, and decision rules then preserve that meaning through analysis.

items.label: Define
items.title: Choose the biological quantity.
items.body: Specify whether the assay measures identity, abundance, uptake, translation, viability, presentation, or function.

items.label: Calibrate
items.title: Establish a meaningful range.
items.body: Document standards, blanks, instrument settings, linear range, detection limits, and acceptance thresholds.

items.label: Normalize
items.title: Preserve the comparison.
items.body: State reference samples, loading or cell-count corrections, batch handling, and transformations.

items.label: Decide
items.title: Predefine interpretation.
items.body: Connect the measurement and uncertainty to an advance, revise, reject, or repeat rule.

sections.title: Keep neighboring claims separate.
sections.summary: Delivery, expression, cell state, presentation, and response should be measured beside one another without being collapsed into one success metric.
body: Related readouts are aligned by sample, dose, time, and batch so that apparent improvement in one dimension cannot hide deterioration in another. A condition with higher encoded signal but unacceptable loss of viability is recorded as a trade-off, not a success.

items.label: M–01
items.title: Product identity and topology
items.body: Size, junction identity, RNase R comparison, purity, recovery, and uncertainty in topology interpretation.

items.label: M–02
items.title: Delivery, expression, viability
items.body: Matched samples, dose and time window, uptake/process control, intended output, and cell-state readout.

items.label: M–03
items.title: Presentation and function
items.body: Sequence-specific display, general activation, antigen-positive/negative targets, response, and non-specific toxicity.

items.label: M–04
items.title: Process and batch quality
items.body: Instrument controls, extraction or staining recovery, plate position, reagent lot, batch reference, missingness, and predefined quality exclusions.

sections.title: A figure must be auditable.
sections.summary: The same checklist applies to positive, negative, and ambiguous results.
body: A figure is released only when the plotted value can be traced to its raw source and when another reader can reconstruct the units, exclusions, replicate structure, and analysis version. The caption states both the supported interpretation and the nearest unsupported claim.

items.label: Source
items.title: Raw file and sample trace
items.body: Link the instrument or image file to sample IDs and notebook records.

items.label: Scale
items.title: Units and normalization
items.body: Name axes, units, transformations, baselines, and any excluded observations.

items.label: Structure
items.title: Replicates and analysis
items.body: State biological n, technical n, error definition, statistical method, and analysis version.

items.label: Boundary
items.title: Accessible interpretation
items.body: Explain the result in text and state what the measurement cannot establish.

next.label: Alternative Platform
next.title: Which experimental context carries the system?

pages.title: Alternative Platform
pages.lede: The host changes expression, safety, cost, and comparability.
pages.boundary: Eligibility and the final experimental platform still require confirmation. This page must remain a concise scope record if the project does not meet the Alternative Platform criteria.

facts.label: Choose
facts.value: The platform answers a project-specific need.

facts.label: Adapt
facts.value: Construct and protocol fit the biological context.

facts.label: Compare
facts.value: Advantages are tested against alternatives.

facts.label: Guard
facts.value: Platform-specific risks and limits are explicit.

sections.title: Use the platform because the question requires it.
sections.summary: The page should explain why a standard bacterial or yeast context cannot answer the selected biological question.
body: For CirCure, candidate expression, processing, presentation, or delivery may require mammalian or cell-free systems. The final page should identify the exact system and distinguish a project necessity from eligibility for a special prize.
If the selected work is not genuinely an alternative platform contribution, the route should state that limit honestly rather than expanding a generic award description.

The platform decision should therefore be reversible and evidence-led: use rapid, controllable systems to answer screening questions, and move into biologically richer contexts only when the next claim requires that context.

sections.title: Document what the context changes.
sections.summary: Construct design, handling, controls, measurement, and safety should be adapted together.
body: Changing the host changes more than a protocol. Source quality, processing assumptions, delivery route, stress response, baseline variability, and the meaning of a negative result are reviewed as one connected adaptation record.

items.label: System
items.title: Define source and state.
items.body: Record cell or extract source, provenance, passage or batch, culture conditions, quality criteria, and relevant biological functions.

items.label: Construct
items.title: Map compatibility constraints.
items.body: Explain translation entry, sequence context, payload size, formulation, delivery, and processing assumptions.

items.label: Control
items.title: Build a fair comparison.
items.body: Use matched payload, process, viability, and host controls that separate platform effects from construct effects.

items.label: Reuse
items.title: Release the adaptation path.
items.body: Provide protocols, troubleshooting, acceptance criteria, and platform-specific limitations for future teams.

sections.title: Show utility, not novelty alone.
sections.summary: A platform page becomes meaningful when it demonstrates an observable advantage, a tradeoff, and reproducible operation.
body: Novelty alone is not the endpoint. The platform must answer a defined project need, outperform or complement a credible alternative on that need, and expose the cost, variability, safety, and transfer limits introduced by the choice.

items.label: Performance
items.title: Relevant readout
items.body: Define the platform-dependent property being measured and its acceptance rule.

items.label: Comparison
items.title: Alternative context
items.body: Compare against a relevant standard, simpler system, or literature-supported baseline.

items.label: Limit
items.title: Transferability
items.body: State what cannot be inferred outside the chosen host, batch, or assay context.

items.label: Reuse
items.title: Reproducible operating envelope
items.body: Release the source criteria, handling window, quality gates, failure modes, and troubleshooting evidence another team would need to reproduce the context.

pages.title: Safety and Security
pages.lede: Risk controls begin before every experiment.
pages.boundary: This page is a planning framework and does not replace institutional review, iGEM forms, local regulation, supervision, or project-specific risk assessment.

facts.label: Identify
facts.value: Hazard, exposure route, affected party, and uncertainty.

facts.label: Reduce
facts.value: Elimination and design controls before PPE.

facts.label: Monitor
facts.value: Training, records, incidents, and review points.

facts.label: Stop
facts.value: Explicit no-go conditions and escalation routes.

sections.title: Name who or what could be harmed.
sections.summary: Risk descriptions should be specific enough to change a construct, protocol, access rule, claim, or implementation plan.
body: Each risk statement identifies a hazard, an exposure or misuse pathway, the affected people or environment, existing controls, residual uncertainty, and the owner of the next review. Generic statements that cannot change a decision are not treated as completed assessment.

items.label: Biological
items.title: Material and host risk
items.body: Chassis, payload, expression product, off-target activity, environmental release, cell line handling, and waste.

items.label: Operational
items.title: Chemical and physical risk
items.body: Reagents, sharps, heat, UV, centrifugation, electrical equipment, transport, storage, and disposal.

items.label: Security
items.title: Information and misuse risk
items.body: Access to materials, sequences, data, code, dual-use interpretation, medical misinformation, and unauthorized claims.

items.label: Governance
items.title: Consent, access, and communication
items.body: Stakeholder records, identifiable material, restricted information, public-facing claims, review authority, and the route for correction or withdrawal.

sections.title: Mitigation should be visible in the artifact.
sections.summary: Where possible, the project changes the design or removes the hazard instead of relying only on procedural reminders.
body: Mitigations are ordered by reliability. Elimination and design constraints are considered first, followed by physical or technical controls, documented responsibility, and finally task-specific PPE; every layer names how its effectiveness will be checked.

items.label: Eliminate
items.title: Avoid unnecessary hazard.
items.body: Choose non-pathogenic systems, safer materials, limited functionality, and the minimum data or material access required.

items.label: Engineer
items.title: Build constraints into the system.
items.body: Use design boundaries, containment, access control, fail-safe operation, and assays that reveal unacceptable cell stress.

items.label: Administer
items.title: Define responsibility.
items.body: Training, supervision, inventories, labels, storage, transport, deviation reporting, and incident escalation must be documented.

items.label: Protect
items.title: Use task-specific PPE.
items.body: PPE remains the final layer and is tied to the actual procedure rather than listed generically.

sections.title: A no-go condition is an engineering output.
sections.summary: The team should predefine when a construct, dose, assay, publication, or implementation claim will not advance.
body: A no-go decision is logged with the triggering evidence, responsible reviewer, immediate containment action, and conditions required for reconsideration. Stopping is presented as a designed outcome rather than an unexplained absence of progress.

items.label: SAFE–01
items.title: Unexpected product or unresolved topology
items.body: Stop downstream interpretation and return to construct identity, purification, or geometry.

items.label: SAFE–02
items.title: Signal coupled to unacceptable cell stress
items.body: Reject the condition; do not optimize only for maximum expression or activation.

items.label: SAFE–03
items.title: Evidence cannot support medical readiness
items.body: Keep therapeutic efficacy, safety, dosing, and clinical claims outside the published conclusion.

items.label: SAFE–04
items.title: Consent or access is unclear
items.body: Do not publish identifiable stakeholder material or restricted records.
